title: Per-task success is never audited against the task's declared difficulty, so shortcut tasks and impossible tasks stay invisible inside the aggregate
problem: My suite gives me one number per run. It cannot tell me that three of my tasks are unsolvable and two are passable without the capability I am trying to measure, so the number moves for reasons I never see.
symptom: A task the team calls easy fails on every model and every run, and a task nobody expected to pass succeeds immediately. Both look like ordinary rows in the results table. The aggregate is stable and wrong, and the defect is only ever found by a human reading transcripts.
why_now: The ABC survey of 17 widely used agentic benchmarks found this class of defect in production suites, including a trivial agent scoring 38% on one of them, and its remedy is stated as advice to benchmark AUTHORS: inspect outliers in pilot experiments. No eval harness ships the audit, so it is a manual step performed once, by the suite's authors, before the suite is used by everyone else for years. The two ingredients are cheap and already half-present: harnesses compute per-task pass rates, and teams informally know which tasks are easy.
existing: A reference or oracle solution per task proves a task is SOLVABLE, which is one of the two directions. It says nothing about a task that is passable WITHOUT the target capability, and it is a per-task artifact rather than a cross-task consistency test.

Null-agent and trivial-agent baselines catch the shortcut direction well, but only for shortcuts the null agent happens to exercise; the difficulty-order anomaly catches shortcuts that need real work of the wrong kind.

Item-response-theory style difficulty ESTIMATED from the observed scores is circular for this purpose: it fits difficulty to the outcomes, so an impossible task is explained rather than flagged. The audit needs a difficulty DECLARED before the run.

evidence.title: Establishing Best Practices for Building Rigorous Agentic Benchmarks (full text, ABC task-validity checks)
evidence.quote: if agents consistently fail on easy tasks, this may indicate that tasks are impossible, whereas if agents only succeed on difficult tasks, it may indicate shortcuts
evidence.note: This is the missing primitive stated as a procedure: compare observed per-task success against the task's declared difficulty and treat a violation as a benchmark defect. It is offered as advice to benchmark authors; nothing in an eval harness computes it.

evidence.title: Establishing Best Practices for Building Rigorous Agentic Benchmarks (full text, Figure 2 task-validity checks)
evidence.quote: These checks uncover design or implementation flaws that can create shortcuts, which causes false positive evaluation results, or lead to impossible tasks, which causes false negative evaluation results.
evidence.note: Names both directions the anomaly audit catches, which is why a one-sided 'did the score go up' gate cannot substitute for it.

evidence.title: Establishing Best Practices for Building Rigorous Agentic Benchmarks
evidence.quote: Such issues can lead to under- or overestimation of agents' performance by up to 100% in relative terms.
evidence.note: Classified survey-aggregate, NOT peer-reviewed: as fetched, the arXiv abs page (v5) lists no venue. It synthesises a survey of best practices plus an assessment of 17 widely used agentic benchmarks, which is what earns the non-zero weight.

evidence.title: Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Software Tasks (full text, Appendix F.2 Messiness factors)
evidence.quote: Controlling for task length, we find models perform worse on tasks that have higher messiness scores.
evidence.note: The authors had to INVENT a 16-factor realism attribute and label tasks by hand to make this measurable, because no benchmark task record carries one. That the effect is real (and length-independent) is what makes the missing attribute a measurement gap rather than a nicety.

build_hypothesis: One required declared field per task (difficulty tier, or the human time-to-complete a suite may already hold) plus one verb in the harness that ranks observed per-task pass rates against it and lists the inversions with a direction label: an easy task failing everywhere is a suspected impossible task, a hard task passing everywhere is a suspected shortcut. It needs no new data collection, runs on results a harness already computes, and turns a one-off authoring step into a per-run gate.

check.manual_question: Does anything in your eval pipeline compare each task's OBSERVED pass rate against a difficulty declared before the run, and surface the inversions in both directions - an easy task that fails everywhere as a suspected impossible task, a hard task that passes everywhere as a suspected shortcut?
check.rationale: Fires when a repo computes per-task or suite pass rates while no task record anywhere declares a difficulty for them to be compared against, which is the precondition that makes the audit impossible rather than merely unimplemented. mitigated_when demands BOTH a difficulty notion and anomaly vocabulary in code that runs, because a difficulty field nobody audits is a label, not a check. What it can get wrong: a project that declares difficulty under a different name (tier, complexity, level, an expected pass rate) reads as PRESENT when the audit is in fact possible; and a repo whose only 'difficulty' string sits in an unrelated model-config docstring reads as mitigated if it also happens to spell 'outlier' elsewhere, so a MANUAL verdict here is worth more than the PRESENT one.
